titleText.es: Empecé a hacer las tablas de más gente famosa, pero resultó tan deprimente y morboso que tuve que salir fuera. El tipo del sombrero gana otra vez.
titleText.en: I started to do the tables for more famous people but it got really depressing and morbid and I had to go outside. Hat guy wins again.
titleText.noteEn: The official title is Actuarial, an adjective, while the Spanish archive title Actuario names the professional. The Spanish body also adapts the official description of repeated comment spam as se puso a escribir, while preserving the same trolling setup.

regions.labelEs: SÉ QUE NO HAY QUE ALIMENTAR AL TROLL, PERO ES QUE ALGUNAS VECES ME PROVOCAN TANTO QUE NO PUEDO EVITAR RESPONDER.

applications.explanationEn: Hay que states a general requirement, and alimentar stays in its unchanged -ar dictionary form.
Alimentar supplies the feeding metaphor, and al troll names the online provocateur whose behavior would be rewarded with attention.
Al combines a and el before troll because the troll is treated as a specific person directly affected by alimentar.
Es que opens the speaker's explanation for the contrast introduced by pero.

applications.exampleEs: PROVOCAN TANTO QUE NO PUEDO EVITAR RESPONDER
applications.explanationEn: Provocan names the repeated action, tanto raises its degree, que introduces the consequence, and no puedo evitar responder supplies that complete result.
No and puedo express inability, evitar supplies the idea of preventing the action, and responder stays in its unchanged dictionary form as that action.

regions.labelEs: SÍ, A MÍ TAMBIÉN. AYER UN TÍO SE PUSO A ESCRIBIR "¡PRIMERO!", ASÍ QUE COGÍ ALGUNAS TABLAS DE MORTALIDAD Y ME PASÉ VEINTE MINUTOS DICIÉNDOLE CUÁNDO MORIRÍAN PROBABLEMENTE TODOS LOS HÉROES DE SU INFANCIA.

applications.explanationEn: A introduces the emphasized form mí, and también marks that the same experience applies to the speaker.
Se matches the third-person subject, puso carries the completed past time, a supplies the required link, and escribir remains in its unchanged -ir dictionary form.
Así que introduces the response that follows from the preceding behavior.
Me and pasé form the first-person past of pasarse, veinte minutos gives the duration, and diciéndole names the continuing activity in its -iendo form.
Le is joined to the end of diciendo, and the added written accent preserves the original stress.

applications.exampleEs: CUÁNDO MORIRÍAN PROBABLEMENTE TODOS LOS HÉROES DE SU INFANCIA
applications.explanationEn: Cuándo asks about the unknown time inside a larger telling statement, so it keeps its written accent; the remaining words form the complete embedded question about the heroes' likely deaths.

applications.exampleEs: ME PASÉ VEINTE MINUTOS DICIÉNDOLE CUÁNDO MORIRÍAN PROBABLEMENTE TODOS LOS HÉROES DE SU INFANCIA
applications.explanationEn: Me pasé fixes the telling in completed past time, diciéndole names the reporting act, cuándo opens its embedded question, and morirían places the complete death prediction later than that past viewpoint.
Probable takes the ending -mente to form a word that describes the likelihood of the action.

excludedUnits.rationale: The three dots form a silent reaction mark rather than a Spanish lexical word.

regions.labelEs: RECUÉRDAME QUE NUNCA JAMÁS TE MOLESTE.

applications.explanationEn: Recuerda is the positive command form used with one familiar listener.
Me attaches to the end of the positive command recuerda, and the written accent preserves the command's original stress.
Nunca and jamás reinforce one another to make the negative emphatic.
The unspoken subject is the speaker, and moleste is the special form used for the pending action in the reminder rather than a polite command to the listener.

regions.labelEs: 2038: MUERE EL ÚLTIMO ACTOR DE LA STAR WARS ORIGINAL.

excludedUnits.rationale: 2038 is a calendar year written as digits, not a Spanish lexical word occurrence.
STAR WARS is an English-language film title preserved as a proper name, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Último comes before actor and uses the masculine singular -o ending to match it.
The feminine article points to an understood feminine word for the work, such as película; the English title itself remains unchanged.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: one must; it is necessary (as part of hay que)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something has to be done without naming who must do it?
cards.answerEn: Use hay que followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Hay que does not change for a person; it gives a general requirement, like English “one must,” “you have to,” or “we need to.”

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links hay to the required action

cards.questionEn: What does alimentar al troll mean in an online discussion?
cards.answerEn: It means to engage with a provocateur in a way that rewards or encourages more provocation.
cards.noteEn: Alimentar literally means “to feed,” but this internet expression uses feeding as a metaphor for giving a troll the attention they seek. Al combines a and el before the person being fed. The phrase often appears in advice such as no alimentes al troll.

example.es: Ignora el mensaje; no alimentes al troll.
example.en: Ignore the message; do not feed the troll.

cards.answerEn: a + el before a specific person; often “the” or “to the” in English
cards.noteEn: Spanish contracts a + el to al. The personal a can mark a specific person who receives or is affected by an action; English may use “the,” “to the,” or no separate preposition, depending on the verb.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.
Spanish uses the borrowed noun troll for someone who posts provocative messages mainly to upset people or attract angry replies. This sense is different from the creature in folklore.

example.es: El foro bloqueó a un troll.
example.en: The forum blocked an internet troll.

cards.answerEn: “First post” is a deliberately low-effort internet comment whose main purpose is to claim the first comment slot rather than contribute to the discussion.
cards.noteEn: It can appear as “first,” “first post,” or an exaggerated or deliberately misspelled variant. The cliché is commonly associated with trolling because it seeks attention without adding useful content.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of es que

cards.questionEn: How can you introduce an explanation, excuse, or hesitant objection?
cards.answerEn: Start with es que, then give the explanation.
cards.noteEn: Es que often softens what comes next, especially when the speaker is explaining a problem or pushing back politely. The phrase functions as a unit; its meaning is not obtained by translating es and que separately.

example.es: No puedo ir; es que trabajo esta tarde.
example.en: I can't go; the thing is, I work this afternoon.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of es que

cards.noteEn: In frequency expressions such as a veces and algunas veces, English commonly translates the whole expression as “sometimes.”
Provocan is the present form of provocar for a plural subject. A nearby object word such as me or te identifies the person being provoked.

example.es: Esos mensajes provocan a los lectores.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone does an action so much that a particular result follows?
cards.answerEn: Use the action verb, then tanto, then que before the result.
cards.noteEn: The plus signs in the prompt mean “followed by.” The action verb changes for the person and time, while tanto stays unchanged when it describes the degree of an action. Que introduces the consequence. This differs from tan, which normally comes before a describing word such as difícil.

example.es: Trabajó tanto que se quedó dormido.
example.en: He worked so much that he fell asleep.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a result connector

cards.promptEs: no poder evitar + nombre o verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone cannot help doing an action or cannot avoid a feeling?
cards.answerEn: Use no, a form of poder, evitar, and then the action or feeling that cannot be avoided.
cards.noteEn: Only poder changes for the person and time; evitar remains in its unchanged dictionary form. Another action also stays in its dictionary form: no puedo evitar reír means “I cannot help laughing.” A noun can follow instead, as in no pudo evitar la duda.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces an emphasized object such as a mí
cards.noteEn: A stressed form such as a mí can repeat a short object pronoun such as me for contrast or emphasis. English normally expresses the emphasis through stress rather than an extra word.

example.en: You cannot see me in particular.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “me too” when the same statement applies to you?
cards.noteEn: Mí is the stressed form of “me” used after a, and it carries a written accent. The complete expression can stand alone as a reply or be followed by a repeated verb. The a has no separate English word in the natural reply “me too.”

cards.answerEn: me (after a preposition such as para)
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses mí after most prepositions. The written accent distinguishes mí (“me”) from mi (“my”).

Tío literally means “uncle,” but in informal Spanish from Spain it can also refer to a man or guy. With an article, as in un tío, it normally names someone; used directly to a listener, it can instead work like informal “man” or “dude.”

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks ponerse a, “to start doing”
cards.noteEn: In ponerse a, the small pronoun changes with the person: me pongo, te pones, se pone, nos ponemos, os ponéis, or se ponen. English normally expresses the full construction as “start” or “get down to.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone starts or gets down to doing an action?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching small pronoun and a form of poner, then a, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The small pronoun changes with the person: me pongo, te pones, se pone, nos ponemos, os ponéis, or se ponen. Poner also changes for the person and time. The final action stays in its dictionary form, the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir.

example.es: Después de cenar, nos ponemos a estudiar.

cards.noteEn: Puso is a past form of poner. In se puso a followed by an action verb in its unchanged dictionary form, the complete pattern means that someone started doing that action.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links ponerse to the action that begins
cards.noteEn: Ponerse a requires a before the following action verb. English expresses the full construction as “start doing” and does not translate this a separately.
Primero can claim or state first position in an order or ranking. With a movement verb such as ir, it can describe the current leader: va primero means that a person or team is in first place.

example.es: Daniel va primero en la carrera.

cards.answerEn: so; therefore (as part of así que)

cards.questionEn: How do you connect a situation to its result with “so”?
cards.answerEn: Use así que before the result.
cards.noteEn: Así que joins a cause or situation to what follows from it. The two words work together as one connector; translating así and que separately will not give the intended meaning.

example.es: Está lloviendo, así que llevo un paraguas.
example.en: It is raining, so I am carrying an umbrella.

cards.noteEn: Cogí is the completed past form of coger for the speaker. Coger is ordinary for taking or picking something up in Spain, but it has a vulgar sexual meaning in parts of Latin America, where tomar or agarrar may be preferred.

example.es: Cogí un libro de la mesa.
example.en: I picked up a book from the table.

cards.answerEn: Mortality tables summarize death rates by age or group; actuaries use them to estimate life expectancy and financial risk.
cards.noteEn: The tables describe probabilities across populations, not exact death dates for particular people. Turning them into precise predictions about named people's deaths exaggerates what the statistics can do and makes the calculation deliberately morbid.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone spends a stretch of time doing an activity?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching short word and a form of pasar, name the time period, then add the activity in its -ando or -iendo form.
cards.noteEn: The short word and pasar change with the person: me paso, te pasas, se pasa, nos pasamos. The final activity form describes what fills the time; it commonly ends in -ando or -iendo, as in leyendo, “reading.”

example.es: Lucía se pasa la tarde leyendo.

cards.promptEs: verbo o contexto en pasado + que/cuándo/etc. + forma en -ría
cards.questionEn: How do you report that something was still in the future at an earlier point in time?
cards.answerEn: Set the reporting viewpoint in the past, introduce the reported statement or question, and put the later action or state in a Spanish 'would' form.
cards.noteEn: A past verb, or surrounding words that clearly place the report in the past, establishes the earlier viewpoint. Que can introduce a reported statement, while an accented question word such as cuándo or dónde can introduce an embedded question. The later verb uses the conditional—the form usually made by keeping its dictionary form and adding -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían—to show what would happen or be true after that past point.

example.es: Lucía dijo que llegaría el lunes.
example.en: Lucía said she would arrive on Monday.

cards.answerEn: I spent (time doing something, as part of me pasé)
cards.noteEn: Pasé is a completed past form of pasar. With me and a stated period, me pasé describes how long the speaker spent doing an activity; the activity can follow in a form ending in -ando or -iendo.

Diciendo is the -iendo form of decir used for an activity in progress, and le is attached to identify the recipient. The written accent keeps the original stress after le is added. In other contexts, le can mean “to her” or polite “to you.”

example.es: Siguió diciéndole la verdad a Pablo.
example.en: She kept telling Pablo the truth.

cards.questionEn: How do you attach a word such as “it,” “him,” “her,” or “them” to an ongoing-action form?
cards.answerEn: Join lo, la, los, las, or another object marker to the end of the verb's -ando or -iendo form, adding a written accent when needed to preserve the original stress.
cards.noteEn: The -ando or -iendo form, often called a gerund, presents an action in progress or alongside another action. An object marker can follow it as one written word: haciendo becomes haciéndolo, and leyendo becomes leyéndola. The accent shows that the stressed syllable has not shifted after the extra syllable is added.
Cuándo has an accent when it asks, directly or indirectly, at what time something happens.

cards.questionEn: When “what,” “how,” or “where” introduces unknown information inside a larger sentence, does Spanish keep the written accent?
cards.answerEn: Yes. Keep the accent in qué, cómo, dónde, cuándo, cuál, or quién even when the question is embedded inside a statement.
cards.noteEn: An embedded, or indirect, question reports what is unknown rather than asking it as a separate sentence. It may have no question marks, but the question word still carries its accent. Compare no sé dónde vive, “I don't know where she lives,” with the relative form donde in la casa donde vive, “the house where she lives.”

example.en: I don't know where she lives.

cards.noteEn: Morirían keeps the dictionary form morir and adds -ían. This form is called the conditional; it can place an expected death later than an earlier past viewpoint, as English uses “would die.”

example.es: Pensaban que las plantas morirían sin agua.
example.en: They thought the plants would die without water.

cards.noteEn: Probablemente combines probable with -mente to describe a claim as likely rather than certain.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.
Su agrees with the possessed thing, not with the owner. The same Spanish form can mean his, her, its, their, or formal your; the surrounding context identifies the owner.
Recuerda is the positive command of recordar for one familiar listener. Me attaches to the end, and the written accent keeps the original stress: recuerda + me becomes recuérdame.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.promptEs: imperativo afirmativo de tú + pronombre al final
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: A positive command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. With one informal listener, sienta + te becomes siéntate. A written accent may be added so the combined word keeps the original stress. In a negative command, the short word goes before the verb instead: no te sientes.
cards.questionEn: If a positive command includes a short word such as te (“yourself”) or lo (“it”), where does that word go?
How do you strengthen “never” to mean “never ever”?
cards.answerEn: Use nunca jamás for an emphatic “never ever.”
cards.noteEn: Nunca and jamás can each express “never.” Putting them together intensifies the refusal or promise; Spanish negative words reinforce one another rather than canceling each other. The expression can appear before or after the verb according to the ordinary rules for Spanish negatives.

example.en: I will never ever go back there.

cards.noteEn: Jamás can mean “never” by itself. After nunca, it reinforces the negative and makes nunca jamás mean an emphatic “never ever”; the two negative words do not cancel each other in Spanish.

example.en: I will never ever say that.

cards.noteEn: Before a noun, último can mean the final or last remaining one, or simply the most recent one. The surrounding noun and situation distinguish those readings: el último superviviente is the last survivor, while mi último trabajo can mean my latest work.

cards.promptEs: número ordinal antes de un sustantivo
cards.questionEn: How do you use words such as first, second, or third before a Spanish noun?
cards.answerEn: Put the ordinal before the noun and make its ending match the noun's gender and number.
cards.noteEn: An ordinal gives a position in an order. Primero, segundo, tercero, último, and similar words usually come before the noun. Most forms use -o with a masculine singular noun and -a with a feminine singular noun, but primero and tercero shorten to primer and tercer before a masculine singular noun. Plural nouns use plural forms.

example.es: La segunda puerta está en el tercer piso.
example.en: The second door is on the third floor.

cards.answerEn: argh!; a cry of distress or frustration
cards.noteEn: Argh represents a nonverbal cry in writing. Its spelling varies, but it signals pain, dread, frustration, or disgust rather than naming an action.
